lead: A model is a small copy of a real machine — a spillway, a ship, a pipe network. Testing the copy is cheap; testing the real thing is not. But a measurement on the model only predicts the prototype if the two flows are similar in shape, in velocity pattern and in force ratios. That set of conditions is called similitude. This chapter shows what each similarity fixes, how the scale ratios for velocity, discharge and force follow from the one dimensionless group you match, and why river and harbour models are deliberately built with two different length scales.
prereq: You need the named groups from 5.7, the idea of a π group from 5.6, and Reynolds number in pipes from Unit 4.

blocks.text: The real machine is the prototype (subscript p). The test copy is the model (subscript m). Similitude is the set of conditions that lets a model reading be carried back to the prototype.

Geometric similarity. Every length in the model has the same ratio to the matching length in the prototype. Define the length ratio L_r = L_p / L_m, where L_p is a prototype length in metres and L_m the matching model length in metres. One number then fixes everything: area ratio = L_r², volume ratio = L_r³. The model must have the same shape, not merely the same proportions in one plane.

Kinematic similarity. Velocity at matching points must be in a fixed ratio V_r = V_p / V_m, and so must acceleration. Streamlines then look the same in both, and a particle takes time in the ratio T_r = L_r / V_r. Kinematic similarity is what makes a photograph of the model look like a photograph of the prototype.

Dynamic similarity. Forces at matching points must be in a fixed ratio. Inertia, viscous, gravity and surface-tension forces cannot be scaled independently, so the only clean way to say it is: every dimensionless force ratio must be equal in model and prototype. From 5.7 each group is exactly such a ratio, so matching the group that matters matches the force balance.
A model that matches all three is a true similitude. In practice you match one group — the one whose forces dominate — and this is called the model law.

sections.h3: Model laws: build the scale ratios from the group

blocks.text: Write the group for the model, set it equal to the group for the prototype, and solve for V_r. Everything else follows from geometry and from Q = A V.
Froude law: V_p / √(g L_p) = V_m / √(g L_m)  →  V_r = √L_r
blocks.where: V_r = V_p/V_m is the velocity ratio; L_r = L_p/L_m is the length ratio; g = 9.81 m/s² cancels because it is the same in both.

blocks.text: Q_r = L_r² × √L_r = L_r^(5/2) ,   F_r = ρ_r L_r² V_r² = L_r³ ,   T_r = √L_r
blocks.where: Q_r = Q_p/Q_m is the discharge ratio in m³/s per m³/s; F_r = F_p/F_m is the force ratio in N per N (force ratio, not the Froude number Fr); ρ_r = 1 when the same fluid is used; T_r = T_p/T_m is the time ratio.

blocks.text: Reynolds law, same fluid: V_r = 1 / L_r ,   Q_r = L_r ,   F_r = 1
blocks.where: Re = V L / ν must be equal; ν is the kinematic viscosity in m²/s. Since ν_r = 1, the velocity ratio inverts: the small model must run faster.

blocks.text: The Mach row assumes the same gas at the same temperature, so the sound speed c is unchanged and V_r = 1. The Weber row assumes the same liquid, so surface tension σ is unchanged.

An undistorted model uses one length ratio for all three directions. A distorted model uses a different vertical scale L_vr and horizontal scale L_hr. River and harbour models are almost always distorted, because a 2 km reach that is 30 m deep at 1:1000 would be 2 m long and only 3 cm deep — too shallow for surface tension and viscosity to stay out of the way.
In a distorted model the Froude law is enforced on the vertical plane only, using L_vr. Gravity waves in the model still travel at √(g × depth), so the correct ratios are:
V_r = √L_vr ,   Q_r = L_hr × L_vr^(3/2) ,   S_r = L_vr / L_hr
blocks.where: L_vr is the vertical length ratio, L_hr the horizontal length ratio, Q_r the discharge ratio, and S_r = S_p/S_m the slope ratio. For L_vr = 100 and L_hr = 1000, S_r = 0.1, so the model slope is 10 times steeper than the prototype.

blocks.text: Scale effect is the leftover error. Matching Re and Fr together needs √L_r = 1/L_r, which is true only at L_r = 1 — full size. So the small groups are dropped and the resulting error is estimated and stated. In a 1:30 spillway model, surface tension and viscosity are negligible and Fr alone is enough.

figure.caption: Similitude splits into three matched properties. Dynamic similarity is the branch that matters, and the dominant group selects the model law and all its scale ratios.

spec.aria: A tree with Similitude at the root, branching to Geometric, Kinematic and Dynamic similarity, with Dynamic further branching to the Reynolds law for pipes and submerged bodies, the Froude law for ships and spillways, and the Mach law for compressible flow.

examples.question: A 1:30 scale model of a spillway is tested under Froude similarity. The model velocity is 2.0 m/s, the model discharge is 0.02 m³/s, and the measured force on the model is 15 N. Find the prototype velocity, discharge and force, and state how the times compare. The same water is used in both.
steps: Identify the law. A free-surface flow with gravity waves is controlled by Froude number, so Fr_p = Fr_m. The length ratio is L_r = L_p/L_m = 30, with no unit.
Velocity ratio. V_r = √L_r = √30 = 5.477. Prototype velocity V_p = V_m × V_r = 2.0 × 5.477 = 10.95 m/s, about 10.9 m/s.
Discharge ratio. Q_r = L_r^(5/2) = 30² × √30 = 900 × 5.477 = 4929.5. Prototype discharge Q_p = 0.02 × 4929.5 = 98.6 m³/s.
Force ratio. F_r = ρ_r L_r² V_r². Same water gives ρ_r = 1, and V_r² = L_r, so F_r = L_r³ = 30³ = 27000. Prototype force F_p = 15 × 27000 = 405000 N = 405 kN.
Time ratio. T_r = L_r / V_r = 30 / 5.477 = √L_r = 5.477. So one second in the model represents 5.48 s in the prototype; the model runs faster.
examples.answer: Prototype velocity 10.95 m/s, discharge 98.6 m³/s, force 405 kN, and prototype times are 5.48 times model times.
examples.check:
import math
Lr = 30.0
Vm = 2.0
Qm = 0.02
Fm = 15.0
Vr = math.sqrt(Lr)
Vp = Vm * Vr
Qr = Lr**2.5
Qp = Qm * Qr
Fr = Lr**3
Fp = Fm * Fr
Tr = math.sqrt(Lr)
print(round(Vp, 2))
print(round(Qp, 2))
print(round(Fp, 1))
print(round(Tr, 2))

traps: Scaling the force by L_r² instead of L_r³. Force is ρ A V², so both the area (L_r²) and the velocity squared (L_r² under Froude) scale, giving L_r³.
Applying the Froude law to a full pipe flow or a submerged body. A pipe with no free surface has no gravity waves; Reynolds number controls it, and V_r = 1/L_r, not √L_r.
Defining L_r both ways. Fix L_r = L_p/L_m once and keep it. A ratio written upside down inverts every answer.

In a distorted model, using Q_r = L_r^(5/2) with the vertical scale alone. The correct ratio is Q_r = L_hr × L_vr^(3/2), because the flow cross-section is width (horizontal scale L_hr) times depth (vertical scale L_vr), and velocity scales as √L_vr.
Forgetting the same-fluid assumption. Re similarity with a different fluid gives V_r = ν_r / L_r, not 1/L_r.

quiz.q: Name the three similarities required for a model to predict its prototype, and state what each one fixes.
quiz.a: Geometric fixes all length ratios (L_r, L_r², L_r³); kinematic fixes the velocity and acceleration ratios at matching points; dynamic fixes the force ratios, which means matching the controlling dimensionless group.

quiz.q: Why can the same water model not satisfy Reynolds and Froude similarity at the same time?
quiz.a: Froude needs V_r = √L_r and Reynolds with the same fluid needs V_r = 1/L_r. Equating them gives L_r = 1, that is, full size. For any real scale one group must be sacrificed, and the leftover error is the scale effect.

quiz.q: A 1:50 Froude model of a weir shows a velocity of 1.5 m/s. Find the prototype velocity and the discharge ratio.
A 1:8 Reynolds model of an oil pipe uses the same oil. The prototype velocity is 1.2 m/s. Find the model velocity and the force ratio.
quiz.a: V_r = 1/L_r = 1/8, so V_m = V_p / V_r = 1.2 × 8 = 9.6 m/s. With the same fluid F_r = ρ_r L_r² V_r² = 1 × 64 × (1/64) = 1, so model and prototype forces are equal.

quiz.q: A river model uses a vertical scale of 1:100 and a horizontal scale of 1:1000. Explain which length ratio sets the discharge ratio and why.
quiz.a: The vertical scale sets velocity, because gravity waves travel at √(g × depth): V_r = √L_vr = √100 = 10. Discharge is flow area × velocity, and the flow area is width (horizontal scale L_hr) × depth (vertical scale L_vr). So Q_r = L_hr × L_vr × √L_vr = L_hr × L_vr^(3/2) = 1000 × 1000 = 10⁶. Using L_vr for both directions gives 100^(5/2) = 10⁵, which underestimates discharge by a factor of 10.

quiz.q: A 1:25 Froude model reads 20 N on a spillway gate. Estimate the prototype force, and say why the Froude law is still acceptable here even though viscous forces are not scaled.
quiz.a: F_r = L_r³ = 15625, so F_p = 20 × 15625 = 312500 N = 312.5 kN. Viscous forces are small compared with gravity and inertia forces in a large spillway flow, so the dropped group causes only a small scale effect and the Froude law holds.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern practice validates a model law against computational fluid dynamics before a physical model is even built, and the two are compared to bound the scale effect. Tidal and estuary models remain deliberately distorted because no undistorted scale can keep both depth and plan area workable. Wind-tunnel testing of tall buildings uses the same logic with Reynolds and Mach groups. Search terms that open this up: scale effect, Froude scaling in hydraulic models, and similarity in turbomachinery testing.
